title: Evaluate AI Limitations and Performance
intro: Why AI systems get things wrong and how their performance changes over time: hallucination, non-determinism and uncertainty; data, concept and behavioural drift; model collapse; the metrics and benchmarks used to measure models; and how to choose between human-in-the-loop and automated operation.
objectives: Explain hallucination, non-determinism and uncertainty, and design controls that reduce their impact
Distinguish data, concept, label and behavioural drift, and describe how drift is detected and handled
Explain model collapse, why it threatens rare cases and fairness, and how provenance prevents it
Calculate and interpret accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and false positive rate, and choose thresholds by the cost of errors
Evaluate generative AI with automatic metrics, model judges and human review, and recognise the limits of benchmarks
Choose between human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop and automated execution, and keep oversight meaningful

scenes.title: When models get it wrong
scenes.say: Every AI system is wrong some of the time. The question is how, how often, and what happens next. | This video covers the three reliability limits you must design around: hallucination, non-determinism and uncertainty.

scenes.title: Fluent, specific and wrong

msgs.t: Find me a precedent where an airline was held liable for wrong advice from its website chatbot.
Certainly. In Harland v. Northern Skies Airways [2019] EWCA Civ 482, the Court of Appeal held the airline liable for its chatbot’s misstatement.
That case does not exist. The citation format is perfect; the content is invented.

notes.d: Output that is fluent and plausible but false or unsupported. NIST calls it confabulation.

scenes.say: A lawyer asks a research assistant for a precedent. | The answer looks perfect: a case name, a year, a court and a neutral citation in the right format. | But the case doesn’t exist. The model produced the most plausible-looking answer, not a verified one. This is hallucination, which the NIST generative AI profile calls confabulation.

scenes.title: Why hallucinations happen

items.d: Models predict likely text; nothing checks it against reality
Facts missing from training, or newer than the cut-off
Training and benchmarks often favour a guess over “I don’t know”
Vague prompts, or retrieval that returns the wrong passages
One wrong step early in a long answer or agent task carries forward

scenes.say: Why does this happen? | First, models are trained to produce plausible continuations of text. Nothing in that process checks a claim against the real world. | Second, the facts may simply be missing: too rare in the training data, or newer than the training cut-off. | Third, training and many benchmarks reward a confident guess more than an honest “I don’t know”, so models learn to guess. | Fourth, a vague prompt, or retrieval that returns the wrong passages, leaves the model filling gaps. | And in long answers and multi-step agent tasks, one early error carries forward and compounds.

scenes.title: Two kinds of hallucination
rows: Output contradicts the source it was given
Output adds claims the source can’t support
A summary says “approved” when the report says “rejected”
A summary adds a deadline that appears nowhere
Faithfulness checks against the source
Require citations; verify or remove unsupported claims
scenes.say: It helps to separate two kinds. | An intrinsic hallucination contradicts the source the model was given. An extrinsic hallucination adds something the source simply doesn’t contain. | For example, a summary that says a request was approved when the report says rejected is intrinsic. A summary that invents a deadline is extrinsic. | Intrinsic errors are caught by checking faithfulness to the source. Extrinsic errors are caught by requiring citations, and verifying or removing anything that has none.

scenes.title: Same prompt, different answers

items.d: Temperature and top-p deliberately add randomness
Floating-point order varies, so even temperature 0 can differ
A provider changes the model behind the same name
Different retrieved passages, tool results or history

scenes.say: The second limit is non-determinism: the same prompt can give different answers. | Sampling settings such as temperature and top-p add randomness on purpose. | Even at temperature zero, outputs can vary, because the order of floating-point operations changes with hardware and with how requests are batched together. | A hosted provider may update the model behind the same name. | And in RAG and agent systems, the retrieved passages, tool results and conversation history differ from run to run.

scenes.title: Two kinds of uncertainty
rows: Noise or ambiguity in the data itself
Gaps in what the model has learned
No: more data won’t remove it
Yes: better or more data can reduce it
A smudged digit that could be a 1 or a 7
Inputs unlike anything seen in training
Report a range or ask for clarification
Retrieve evidence, abstain, or escalate
scenes.say: The third limit is uncertainty, and there are two kinds. | Aleatoric uncertainty comes from noise or ambiguity in the data itself. Epistemic uncertainty comes from gaps in what the model has learned. | More data can’t remove aleatoric uncertainty, but it can reduce epistemic uncertainty. | A smudged digit that could be a one or a seven is aleatoric. An input unlike anything in the training data, such as a new type of attack traffic, is epistemic. | So the responses differ: report a range or ask for clarification for the first, and retrieve evidence, abstain or escalate for the second.

scenes.title: Confidence is not accuracy
scenes.yLabel: Actual accuracy at each stated confidence

notes.d: A calibrated model that says 80% is right about 80% of the time.
Deep networks, and LLMs stating confidence in words, are often overconfident.
Routing to humans by confidence only works if confidence means something.

scenes.say: Models can report a confidence score, but is it trustworthy? A model is well calibrated when its stated confidence matches how often it is actually right. Eighty per cent confidence should mean right about eighty per cent of the time. | Many models are overconfident, and language models that state their confidence in words are often poorly calibrated. | Here, when the model says ninety per cent, it is right only two times in three. That matters, because any design that routes uncertain cases to a human depends on confidence meaning something.

scenes.title: Designing for unreliable output

items.d: Answer from approved sources and cite them
Make “I don’t know” an acceptable, tested answer
Check facts, code and figures before anyone relies on them
Low confidence or high impact goes to a person
Validate before it reaches a system, a customer or a tool

scenes.say: You can’t remove these limits, so you design around them. | Ground answers in approved sources, and require citations. | Make “I don’t know” an acceptable answer, and test that the system actually uses it. | Verify anything that matters, such as facts, figures and generated code, before anyone relies on it. | Route low-confidence or high-impact cases to a person. | And never pass model output straight into another system, a customer message or a tool call without validation. That is the heart of improper output handling and misinformation in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications.

items: Hallucination: plausible but false; intrinsic or extrinsic
Non-determinism: sampling, hardware, updates, context
Uncertainty: aleatoric is noise, epistemic is a knowledge gap
Ground, abstain, verify, route by risk, validate output
scenes.say: To recap. | Hallucination is plausible but false output. Intrinsic hallucinations contradict the source; extrinsic ones add unsupported claims. | Non-determinism comes from sampling, hardware and batching, silent updates and changing context. | Aleatoric uncertainty is noise in the data; epistemic uncertainty is a gap in the model’s knowledge, and only the second shrinks with more data. | And the design response is always similar: ground, allow abstention, verify, route by risk, and validate output before it is used.

blocks.md:
### Hallucination: plausible is not the same as true
A language model generates the most probable continuation of its input. Most of the time, the most probable answer is also the correct one, because correct facts appear often in training data. When the model lacks the fact, it does not stop: it produces whatever *looks* most like a correct answer. The result is **hallucination**: output that is fluent and confident but false, fabricated or unsupported by the source material. The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) uses the term **confabulation** for the same risk.

Two real cases show why this is a business risk, not a curiosity:

- In 2023, lawyers in a US federal case, *Mata v. Avianca*, were sanctioned after filing a brief that cited court decisions a chatbot had invented. The citations looked genuine.
- In 2024, a Canadian tribunal held Air Canada liable after its website chatbot gave a customer wrong information about bereavement fares. The airline argued the chatbot was responsible for its own statements; the tribunal disagreed. **Organisations own what their AI tells people.**

Hallucination also creates security exposure. Code assistants sometimes recommend software packages that do not exist; in one large study, nearly a fifth of the package names suggested by the models tested were invented. Attackers can register those names and fill them with malicious code, an attack sometimes called **slopsquatting**. A reliability limitation becomes a supply-chain vulnerability the moment someone installs what the model suggested without checking.

### Why it happens
- **Objective:** training rewards plausible text, not verified truth.
- **Knowledge gaps:** rare facts, private facts and events after the training cut-off are missing.
- **Incentives:** many training signals and benchmarks score a wrong guess the same as, or better than, an abstention, so models learn to guess rather than say “I don’t know”.
- **Context failures:** ambiguous prompts, or retrieval that returns irrelevant passages, leave gaps that the model fills.
- **Compounding:** in long outputs and multi-step agent tasks, an early error becomes the premise for later steps.

### Intrinsic and extrinsic
An **intrinsic** hallucination contradicts the provided source: a summary reverses a decision, or misstates a number from the document. An **extrinsic** hallucination adds content that the source cannot support: an invented deadline, a fictional reference. Related terms you may see are **faithfulness** (does the output agree with its source?) and **factuality** (is it true in the world?). RAG improves factuality by supplying sources, but it does not guarantee faithfulness: the model can still misread or embellish what it retrieved.

### Non-determinism
Generative models usually *sample* from a probability distribution, so repeated runs can differ by design. Lowering temperature reduces variation but does not remove it: on GPUs, the order of floating-point operations can change with batch size and hardware, which can flip a close decision between two tokens. Hosted providers may also update models, safety filters or system components behind the same API name, and RAG or agent systems see different passages, tool results and histories on each run.

Non-determinism matters for security in three ways:
1. **Testing:** a single passing test proves little. Evaluate many runs and look at the distribution of outcomes, especially for safety tests.
2. **Reproducibility:** investigations need the exact model version, parameters, prompt, retrieved context and output, so log them.
3. **Consistency of decisions:** if two identical cases can receive different outcomes, the process may be unfair and hard to defend. Use low temperature, pinned versions and structured outputs for decision tasks, and keep a human or a deterministic rule as the authority where consistency is required.

### Uncertainty and calibration
**Aleatoric** uncertainty is inherent noise or ambiguity in the data; it can’t be reduced by more training data. **Epistemic** uncertainty reflects what the model doesn’t know; it is high for **out-of-distribution** inputs, such as a new fraud pattern or a language the model rarely saw, and it can be reduced with better data.

A model is **well calibrated** when its confidence matches its accuracy. Calibration is measured with reliability diagrams and the **expected calibration error (ECE)**, the average gap between confidence and accuracy. Modern deep networks tend to be overconfident, and a language model’s *stated* confidence (“I’m 95% sure”) is generated text, not a measurement. Better signals include agreement across several sampled answers (**self-consistency**), token probabilities where the provider exposes them, and verification against sources.

blocks.title: Controls that reduce the impact of unreliable output
items: Grounding and citations

Supply approved sources through retrieval and require the answer to cite them. Check that each claim maps to a cited passage; flag or remove claims that don’t. Grounding reduces extrinsic hallucination but needs a faithfulness check to catch misreadings.
Abstention by design
Instruct and test the system to say when the sources don’t contain the answer. Include unanswerable questions in your evaluation set and measure how often the system correctly declines.
Verification proportional to risk

Low-stakes drafting may need only spot checks. Legal, medical, financial and security content needs verification by a qualified person or a deterministic tool before use. Generated code should pass review, tests and dependency checks before it runs anywhere important.
Consistency controls
Pin model versions, use low temperature and structured output for decision tasks, and record parameters so results can be reproduced. Re-run evaluations after any model, prompt or retrieval change.
Output validation
Treat output as untrusted input to the next system: validate schemas, encode for the destination, check links and package names, and never let unvalidated output trigger an action.

blocks.title: Limitation or vulnerability?
blocks.md: A hallucination is a **model limitation**: it happens without an attacker. It becomes a **security issue** when someone can exploit it (registering hallucinated package names) or when the output drives an action without validation. In findings and exam scenarios, ask: *is there an adversary or a missing control that turns this limitation into harm?* Domain 6 returns to this distinction.

q.q: A bank’s assistant must answer customer questions about fees accurately. Which design MOST reduces the risk of confident but wrong answers reaching customers?
o: Raise the temperature so the model considers more possible answers before choosing the most likely one
Ground answers in the approved fee schedule, require citations, and decline when the schedule doesn’t cover it
Use the largest model available, because larger models hallucinate far less and can be trusted with fees
Add a clear disclaimer to every answer saying fee information may be wrong and should be checked with a branch first
q.why: Grounding plus citations plus abstention attacks the causes of hallucination and makes errors visible. Larger models still hallucinate, higher temperature increases variation, and a disclaimer shifts blame without reducing harm.

sections.title: Lifecycle degradation: model, data and behavioural drift

scenes.title: Why good models go bad
scenes.sub: Data drift, concept drift and behavioural drift
scenes.say: A model that passed every test on launch day can quietly get worse, without a single line of code changing. | This video explains why models degrade, the main kinds of drift, and how to detect and respond to them.

scenes.title: Performance after deployment
scenes.say: Here is a fraud model’s precision over its first ten months. On launch it is excellent, and then it slowly declines, month after month. | Nothing in the code changed. The world changed: customers, products and fraudsters all moved on, and the patterns the model learned stopped matching reality. | With monitoring in place, the decline is spotted early and the model is retrained on recent data, restoring its performance.

scenes.title: Four kinds of drift

items.d: The inputs change: new customers, devices, languages or products
The meaning changes: the same inputs now lead to different outcomes
The mix of outcomes changes, such as fraud becoming more common
An AI system’s outputs change: updates, prompts, retrieval, tools

scenes.say: Drift comes in four main kinds. | Data drift, also called covariate shift, means the inputs change. New customer groups, devices, languages or products appear that the model rarely saw in training. | Concept drift means the relationship itself changes. The same inputs now lead to a different outcome, for example when fraudsters switch tactics so that yesterday’s safe pattern is today’s fraud. | Label drift, or prior shift, means the mix of outcomes changes, such as fraud becoming twice as common. | And behavioural drift is the change you see in a generative AI system’s outputs when the model, prompts, retrieved content or tools change underneath it.

scenes.title: Spotting data drift
scenes.yLabel: Share of applicants by age band

notes.d: Statistics such as PSI or a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test flag significant shifts.
Input drift is visible immediately, long before outcomes are known.

scenes.say: Data drift is the easiest to spot, because you only need the inputs. Here is the age profile of the applicants the model was trained on. | And here is this month’s production traffic, after a new mobile app attracted far younger applicants. Statistical measures such as the population stability index, or a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, compare the two distributions and raise an alert when the shift is significant. You don’t need to wait for outcomes to know the model is now working outside its experience.

scenes.title: Behavioural drift in generative AI

items.d: A new model version behind the same name
A “small” system-prompt change shifts many answers
New, removed or poisoned documents change retrieval
People use the system for things it was never tested on

scenes.say: Generative AI systems drift in their own ways. | Hosted providers improve and replace models, sometimes behind the same name. A study in twenty twenty-three found one major model’s behaviour on some tasks changed markedly within three months. | A seemingly small edit to a system prompt or configuration can shift thousands of answers. | Changes to the knowledge base change what is retrieved, and a poisoned document changes it deliberately. | And users find new uses the system was never evaluated for.

scenes.title: From detection to response
scenes.say: Detection and response form a pipeline. Production inputs, outputs and eventual outcomes feed monitoring, which runs drift statistics and replays a fixed golden test set against the live system. | When a metric crosses a threshold agreed in advance, an alert fires. | Someone diagnoses the cause, including the security question: is this natural change, or is someone manipulating the inputs or poisoning the data? | The response might be retraining on recent data, recalibrating a threshold, or rolling back to the previous version. | And every fix is re-validated with the same tests used at launch before it is redeployed.

items: Models degrade because the world changes, not the code
Data, concept, label and behavioural drift
Monitor inputs now; outcomes when labels arrive
Diagnose natural vs adversarial; re-validate every fix
scenes.say: To recap. | Models degrade because the world changes around them, even when the code doesn’t. | Watch for data drift, concept drift, label drift and, in generative systems, behavioural drift. | Monitor input distributions immediately, and performance as soon as true outcomes arrive. | Diagnose whether drift is natural or adversarial, and re-validate every fix before it goes back into production.

blocks.md:
### Why models degrade
A trained model is a snapshot of the relationships in its training data. Production is not a snapshot. Customers change, products launch, regulations shift, adversaries adapt, and the model’s assumptions slowly stop matching reality. This **lifecycle degradation** usually happens without any change to the model or code, which is why it so often goes unnoticed.

The COVID-19 pandemic was a dramatic example. In 2020, spending, travel and demand patterns changed almost overnight, and many demand-forecasting and fraud models that had been accurate for years started producing poor results within weeks.

### The kinds of drift
| Drift | What changes | Example | How you see it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Data drift** (covariate shift) | The distribution of inputs | A new app brings younger applicants | Input statistics shift; no labels needed |
| **Concept drift** | The relationship between inputs and outcome | Fraudsters change tactics; old “safe” patterns now indicate fraud | Performance falls once outcomes are known |
| **Label drift** (prior shift) | The mix of outcomes | Fraud rate doubles during a holiday season | Outcome rates change; thresholds misfire |
| **Model drift** | The model’s performance (the symptom) | Precision falls from 92% to 70% | Monitored performance metrics |
| **Behavioural drift** | A generative system’s outputs | A provider update changes refusal behaviour | Golden-set regression tests, output monitoring |

**Model drift** is best thought of as the *symptom*, declining performance, while data, concept and label drift are *causes*. Concept drift can be **sudden** (a new regulation), **gradual** (slowly changing customer behaviour), **incremental**, or **recurring** (seasonal patterns).

### Behavioural drift in generative AI
LLM applications drift in ways traditional models don’t:
- **Provider updates.** Hosted models are improved, re-tuned and replaced. A widely cited 2023 study comparing versions of the same major model a few months apart found large changes in performance on some tasks, including code generation and following formatting instructions.
- **Configuration changes.** System prompts, temperature, safety settings, tool definitions and retrieval parameters are all part of behaviour. Each change can shift outputs across thousands of conversations.
- **Knowledge base changes.** In RAG systems, adding, editing or deleting documents changes answers, and a poisoned document changes them deliberately.
- **Usage drift.** People find new uses, such as a support assistant being used for HR questions, that were never evaluated.

The main controls are **version pinning** (choose when to move to a new model version, rather than having it chosen for you), **change management** for prompts and configuration, and a **golden test set**: a fixed set of representative and adversarial prompts with expected behaviour, re-run on every change and on a schedule.

### Detecting drift
- **Input monitoring.** Compare production inputs to the training baseline with statistics such as the **population stability index (PSI)**, the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test or Jensen–Shannon divergence. For text and images, compare the distribution of embeddings. This needs no labels, so it gives early warning.
- **Output monitoring.** Watch the distribution of predictions, confidence scores, refusal rates, answer lengths and the rate of “I don’t know” responses.
- **Performance monitoring.** Compute accuracy, precision and recall once true outcomes arrive. Outcomes are often delayed (a loan default may take months to appear), so combine late labels with leading indicators such as analyst override rates and complaint volumes.
- **Thresholds and ownership.** Agree alert thresholds, owners and response times before launch, not after the first incident.

### Drift and security
Drift is a security signal as well as a quality one. A sudden shift in inputs might be a marketing campaign, or an attacker probing a model; a sudden change in a RAG system’s answers might be a content update, or poisoning. Every drift investigation should ask whether the change is **natural or adversarial**. Significant drift, model updates and disclosed vulnerabilities are also standard **reassessment triggers** for the risk assessments covered in Domain 2.

### Responding
Typical responses, from lightest to heaviest: recalibrate thresholds; retrain on recent data; roll back to a previous version while investigating; restrict the model’s use to the population it still handles well; or retire it. Whatever the fix, re-run the launch validation suite, including safety and fairness tests, before redeploying.

blocks.title: Drift scenarios
items: Credit scoring

A lender’s new mobile app attracts many younger applicants with thin credit histories. Input monitoring shows a large PSI on age and credit-history length within two weeks. **Drift type:** data drift. **Response:** flag the affected segment for manual review, collect outcomes, and retrain once enough labelled data exists.
Phishing detection

Attackers start using AI-written emails with perfect grammar, which the classifier had learned to treat as a sign of legitimacy. Input statistics look normal, but missed phishing reports rise. **Drift type:** concept drift, adversarially driven. **Response:** retrain with new examples, add features that don’t depend on writing quality, and share indicators with threat intelligence.
Support assistant

After the provider moves the “latest” alias to a new model, the assistant starts answering questions it previously declined, including some outside policy. **Drift type:** behavioural drift. **Response:** pin the previous version, run the golden test set against the new one, and adopt it only after it passes.
Seasonal retail

Return-fraud rates triple every January. The model’s fixed threshold produces a flood of false negatives. **Drift type:** label (prior) drift, recurring. **Response:** seasonal thresholds or retraining that includes previous Januaries, with monitoring tuned to the season.

blocks.title: Causes and symptom
blocks.md: Data, concept and label drift are **causes**. Falling performance (model drift) is the **symptom**. Input monitoring detects some causes early; performance monitoring confirms the symptom, but only once outcomes are known.

q.q: A fraud model’s precision falls steadily for three months. Input feature distributions are unchanged, but fraud analysts report new scam patterns the model misses. Which drift is MOST likely?
o: Data drift
Concept drift
Label drift
No drift; the model has a coding error
q.why: The inputs look the same, but their relationship to the outcome has changed because fraudsters changed tactics. That is concept drift. Data drift would show in the input distributions.

scenes.sub: What happens when models learn from models
scenes.say: More and more of the text and images online are now generated by AI. So what happens when the next generation of models is trained on them? | This video explains model collapse, why it matters for security and fairness, and how to prevent it.

scenes.title: The recursive loop
scenes.centerSub: each generation learns from the last
scenes.intro: Without provenance controls, generated content flows back into training data.

notes.d: A wide spread, including rare but important cases at the edges.
The tails thin out first. Average quality still looks fine.
