scenes.say: Picture all the content a model might produce, from typical cases in the middle to rare ones at the edges. Human-generated data has a wide spread, including rare but important cases. | Train a model on a sample of that data, then train the next model on the first model’s output, and the rare cases begin to disappear, because a finite sample under-represents them every time. This early collapse is hard to notice, because average quality still looks fine. | After many generations, outputs converge on a narrow, repetitive middle that no longer reflects the real world. This is late collapse.

scenes.title: Early and late collapse
rows: Rare events and minority patterns fade
Output converges and loses variety
Benchmarks and averages still look healthy
Repetitive, bland or garbled output
Edge cases are where security and fairness live
The model no longer reflects reality
scenes.say: Researchers distinguish two stages. | In early collapse, rare events and minority patterns fade away. In late collapse, the output converges and loses its variety. | Early collapse is the more dangerous for security teams, because averages and benchmarks still look healthy. Late collapse is obvious: output becomes repetitive, bland or garbled. | And the edge cases that disappear first are exactly where security and fairness live: unusual attack patterns, rare medical conditions, minority dialects and under-represented groups.

scenes.title: Preventing collapse

items.d: Accumulate new data alongside it; never replace it
Label synthetic data at creation and carry the label through
Filter for quality and correctness; cap its share
Test rare cases and diversity, not only averages

scenes.say: Model collapse is preventable. | Keep the original human-generated data, and accumulate new data alongside it rather than replacing it. Research suggests that accumulating data, instead of replacing it, largely avoids collapse. | Track provenance: label synthetic data when it is created, and carry that label through every pipeline. | Use synthetic data deliberately, filtered for quality, verified for correctness, and capped as a share of the training mix. | And evaluate the tails: test rare cases and measure diversity, not just average performance.

items: Collapse: degradation from training on model-generated data
Tails vanish first; averages hide it
Rare cases matter most for security and fairness
Keep human data, track provenance, test the tails
scenes.say: To recap. | Model collapse is the degradation that follows from training models on data generated by other models. | The tails vanish first, while averages hide the problem. | Those rare cases matter most for security and fairness. | So keep the original human data, track the provenance of everything you train on, curate synthetic data, and test the tails.

blocks.md:
### What model collapse is
**Model collapse** is a degenerative process in which models trained on data produced by earlier models progressively lose information about the true data distribution. The effect was demonstrated across language models, image models and simpler statistical models in research published in *Nature* in 2024 by Shumailov and colleagues, building on their 2023 paper *The Curse of Recursion*.

The analogy is a photocopy of a photocopy. Each copy is almost as good as the last, but small losses accumulate until the image is unrecognisable. For models, the first thing lost is the **tails** of the distribution: the rare, unusual and minority cases.

### Why it happens
The research identifies three compounding sources of error:
- **Statistical approximation error.** Every training set is a finite sample. Rare events are under-represented in any sample, and a model trained on that sample reproduces them even less often. Repeat this over generations and they vanish.
- **Functional expressivity error.** Models can’t represent every distribution perfectly, so each generation introduces small distortions.
- **Functional approximation error.** Training procedures are imperfect, adding further bias with each generation.

Each error is small, but recursion compounds them.

### Model collapse is not drift
| | Drift | Model collapse |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | The world changes after training | Training data increasingly comes from models |
| When it appears | In production, over time | In the next model generation |
| Main fix | Monitor and retrain on fresh real data | Protect and accumulate genuine data; track provenance |

It is also different from **catastrophic forgetting**, where a model loses earlier skills when it is trained on new tasks.

### Why security and governance teams care
1. **Rare cases disappear first.** Fraud, intrusions and abuse are, by definition, unusual. A model that has lost its tails misses exactly the events security depends on.
2. **Fairness erodes.** Minority groups, languages and dialects are rare in data. Collapse removes them first, producing biased systems even when the original data was balanced.
3. **Errors become self-reinforcing.** Hallucinated facts that are published and re-scraped become “training truth” for the next model.
4. **Provenance becomes a security property.** Knowing whether data is human-generated, synthetic, or of unknown origin is now essential to training data integrity, a topic Domain 3 covers in depth. Some researchers compare pre-2022 human data to low-background steel: valuable precisely because it predates contamination.
5. **Poisoning at scale.** If attackers can publish large volumes of synthetic content that future scrapers will collect, they can shape future models. Provenance controls defend against collapse and poisoning together.

### Synthetic data is not the enemy
Synthetic data has legitimate uses: augmenting rare classes, generating privacy-preserving test data, creating labelled examples for training, and *distillation*, where a smaller model learns from a larger one. The risk comes from **indiscriminate, recursive, unlabelled** use. Good practice is to:
- record the origin of every dataset and label synthetic records at creation;
- keep original human data and **accumulate** rather than replace;
- verify synthetic data for correctness, filter low-quality output and cap its proportion;
- monitor diversity and tail performance across model generations, not just averages.

blocks.title: Collapse vocabulary
cards: Progressive loss of information about the real data distribution when models train on model-generated data.
The rare, unusual cases at the edges. They are the first to disappear in collapse.
Rare cases fade while average performance still looks normal. Hard to detect.
Output converges on a narrow, repetitive and distorted middle.
Data generated by a model or simulation rather than collected from real events.
A record of where data came from and how it was produced and changed.

blocks.title: Cheaper training data
blocks.md: A support-automation team wants to cut labelling costs. Their plan: generate 2 million synthetic support conversations with the current model, discard the older human transcripts to save storage, and train the next model on the synthetic set. Their benchmark, average answer quality, is expected to stay the same.

q.q: What is the BEST advice to the team?
o: Proceed, since average answer quality will be unaffected and synthetic data is cheaper to maintain
Keep the human transcripts, label and cap the synthetic data, verify its quality, and test rare, hard cases
Replace the human transcripts with synthetic data generated by a different vendor’s model, for diversity
Increase the synthetic set to 20 million conversations so the volume compensates for any loss of quality
q.why: Replacing real data with recursive synthetic data invites model collapse, and average-quality benchmarks hide early collapse. Keeping and accumulating human data, tracking provenance, controlling the synthetic share and testing the tails are the recognised mitigations. More synthetic data, or another model’s output, does not fix the underlying problem.

q.q: Why is early model collapse particularly hard to detect?
o: It only affects image models, which most security teams don’t monitor closely
Rare cases vanish first, while average metrics and benchmarks still look healthy
It makes the model stop responding entirely, which looks like an ordinary outage
It shows up only in the model’s source code, which most organisations can’t inspect
q.why: Early collapse removes the tails of the distribution first. Because rare cases contribute little to averages, standard metrics look normal unless you specifically test rare cases and diversity.

scenes.title: Measuring a classifier
scenes.sub: Confusion matrices, precision, recall and the accuracy trap
scenes.say: You can’t manage what you can’t measure, and with AI, choosing the wrong measure can hide a dangerous model behind a great-looking number. | This video covers the core metrics for classifiers, the kind of model behind malware detection, fraud scoring and alert triage.

scenes.title: The confusion matrix
rows: Actually malicious
Actually benign

notes.d: Malicious and missed. The dangerous error.
Benign but flagged. Costs analyst time.

scenes.say: Every metric starts from the confusion matrix. Here, a malware detector scans ten thousand files, of which one hundred are actually malicious. | Ninety malicious files are flagged. These are true positives. | Ten malicious files are missed. These false negatives are the dangerous error. | Forty-five harmless files are flagged by mistake. These false positives cost analyst time and erode trust. | And nine thousand eight hundred and fifty-five harmless files are correctly left alone. These are true negatives.

num.label: accuracy for a “detector” that never flags anything at all

scenes.def: When only 1% of files are malicious, flagging nothing is 99% accurate, and catches no malware.
scenes.ex: Our real detector scores 99.45% accuracy. The number tells you almost nothing about how well it finds malware.
scenes.say: Now a trap. A detector that never flags anything at all scores ninety-nine per cent accuracy on this data. | Because only one per cent of files are malicious, doing nothing is right ninety-nine times in a hundred, while catching no malware whatsoever. This is the accuracy paradox, and it applies to every rare-event problem in security. | Our real detector scores ninety-nine point four five per cent. That number barely distinguishes it from a detector that does nothing.

scenes.title: The metrics that matter

items.d: 90 ÷ 135 = 67%. Of the alerts, how many are real?
90 ÷ 100 = 90%. Of the real threats, how many were caught?
2PR ÷ (P + R) = 77%. One number that balances the two
45 ÷ 9,900 = 0.45%. Small rates still flood analysts at scale

scenes.say: Four metrics tell the real story. | Precision asks: of everything flagged, how much was really malicious? Ninety out of one hundred and thirty-five, or sixty-seven per cent. | Recall, also called sensitivity or the true positive rate, asks: of all the real malware, how much did we catch? Ninety out of a hundred, or ninety per cent. | F1 combines them, using the harmonic mean, so it is only high when both are high. Here it is seventy-seven per cent. | And the false positive rate is the share of harmless items wrongly flagged. Point four five per cent sounds tiny, but across ten million files a day, it is forty-five thousand false alarms.

scenes.title: The threshold trade-off

notes.d: Most classifiers output a score. The threshold turns it into a decision.
Catches more threats, raises more false alarms.
Fewer, better alerts, but more misses.

scenes.say: Most classifiers output a score, and a threshold turns that score into a decision. Move the threshold, and precision and recall trade against each other. | Lower it, and you catch more threats at the cost of more false alarms. That suits problems where a miss is very costly, such as ransomware or fraud. | Raise it, and the alerts you get are more reliable, but more threats slip through. Choosing the threshold is a business and risk decision, not just a technical one.

scenes.title: Which metric to prioritise
rows: Catch as many real cases as possible
Raise as few false alarms as possible
Missing a case is very costly
Each alert is expensive to handle
Ransomware, fraud, data exfiltration
Automated blocking of customer logins
scenes.say: So which matters more? | Prioritise recall when you need to catch as many real cases as possible. Prioritise precision when you need as few false alarms as possible. | Recall wins when a miss is very costly. Precision wins when every alert is expensive, or when the system acts automatically. | Ransomware and exfiltration detection usually favour recall. A system that automatically blocks customer logins needs high precision, because every false positive locks out a real customer.

items: Start from the confusion matrix: TP, FP, FN, TN
Accuracy misleads when the event is rare
Precision: alert quality; recall: threats caught
The threshold sets the trade-off; choose it by cost
scenes.say: To recap. | Every metric comes from the confusion matrix: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. | Accuracy misleads whenever the event you care about is rare. | Precision measures the quality of alerts; recall measures how many real threats you catch. | And the threshold sets the trade-off between them, so choose it by the cost of each kind of error.

blocks.md:
### The confusion matrix
For a binary classifier, every prediction lands in one of four cells. Using the malware example from the video (10,000 files, 100 malicious):

| | Flagged (predicted positive) | Not flagged (predicted negative) |
|---|---|---|
| **Actually malicious** | True positive (TP) = 90 | False negative (FN) = 10 |
| **Actually benign** | False positive (FP) = 45 | True negative (TN) = 9,855 |

A **false positive** is also called a *type I error*; a **false negative** is a *type II error*.

### The core metrics
| Metric | Formula | Example | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | (TP + TN) ÷ total | 9,945 ÷ 10,000 = 99.45% | How often is the model right overall? |
| Precision | TP ÷ (TP + FP) | 90 ÷ 135 = 66.7% | When it raises an alert, how often is it real? |
| Recall (sensitivity, TPR) | TP ÷ (TP + FN) | 90 ÷ 100 = 90% | Of the real threats, how many did it catch? |
| Specificity (TNR) | TN ÷ (TN + FP) | 9,855 ÷ 9,900 = 99.5% | Of the harmless items, how many were left alone? |
| False positive rate | FP ÷ (FP + TN) | 45 ÷ 9,900 = 0.45% | How often is a harmless item flagged? |
| F1 score | 2 × P × R ÷ (P + R) | 2 × 0.667 × 0.9 ÷ 1.567 = 76.6% | A single balance of precision and recall |

**Base rates matter.** Precision depends heavily on how common the positive class is. The same detector applied to a population where malware is ten times rarer would raise roughly the same number of false alarms but find a tenth of the threats, so its precision would collapse. Always evaluate on data with realistic proportions.

### Thresholds, ROC and PR curves
Most classifiers output a score between 0 and 1. The **decision threshold** converts it to a yes or no. Lowering the threshold raises recall and the false positive rate; raising it improves precision and lowers recall.

- A **ROC curve** plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across all thresholds. The **area under the curve (AUC)** summarises it: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is no better than chance. AUC measures ranking quality independent of any one threshold.
- A **precision–recall (PR) curve** plots precision against recall. For rare events, the PR curve is more informative than ROC, because a tiny false positive rate can still mean many false alarms.
- Because the right threshold depends on the cost of each error, it should be set with the business owner. A security team might express it as: “maximise recall while keeping alert volume within the capacity of the analysts.”

### Beyond classification
- **Regression** (predicting a number, such as transaction value or capacity demand) uses **mean absolute error (MAE)**, the average size of errors, and **root mean squared error (RMSE)**, which penalises large errors more heavily.
- **Calibration** (Section 1) measures whether scores can be read as probabilities. A well-ranked model can still be badly calibrated.
- **Fairness metrics** compare error rates across groups. A model with excellent overall recall can still miss far more cases for one group than another. Domain 2 covers fairness measures.
- **Operational metrics** such as latency, throughput, cost per prediction and availability matter as much as accuracy in production.

### Evaluate honestly
Good evaluation uses a **held-out test set** that the model never saw in training or tuning, drawn from the same population the model will face in production. Splitting by time (train on older data, test on newer) is more realistic for security problems, because attackers change over time. Watch for **data leakage**, where information about the answer slips into the training features, producing results that look excellent and then fail in production.

blocks.title: Work the numbers: a phishing filter
items: The data
A phishing filter is tested on 20,000 emails, of which 400 are phishing. It flags 500 emails, of which 360 are phishing.
Fill the matrix
Precision
360 ÷ 500 = 72%. Just over seven in ten flagged emails really are phishing.
Recall
360 ÷ 400 = 90%. The filter catches nine in ten phishing emails and misses 40.
Accuracy
(360 + 19,460) ÷ 20,000 = 99.1%. Impressive-sounding, and nearly useless as a guide.
Decide
If the 40 missed emails could each lead to a breach, the team should lower the threshold to raise recall, then manage the extra alerts with triage automation or more analyst capacity.

blocks.title: Reading metric questions
blocks.md:
- “Of the alerts, how many were real?” is **precision**.
- “Of the real attacks, how many were detected?” is **recall** (sensitivity, true positive rate).
- “Rare event and high accuracy” is a warning sign: think **accuracy paradox**.
- “Costly misses” points to **recall**; “costly false alarms” or “automatic action” points to **precision**.

q.q: A security team’s intrusion classifier reports 99.7% accuracy. Intrusions make up 0.3% of the events it sees. What should the team conclude?
o: The classifier is excellent and ready for production, since 99.7% exceeds the usual 95% benchmark for security tools
Accuracy says little here: predicting “no intrusion” every time would also score 99.7%, so check recall and precision
The classifier is overfitted to the training data and must be retrained on a balanced dataset before use
The classifier’s false positive rate must be exactly 0.3%, matching the share of events that are intrusions
q.why: With a 0.3% base rate, a model that never detects anything scores 99.7% accuracy. Recall shows how many intrusions are caught, and precision shows how reliable the alerts are.

sections.title: Evaluating generative AI: metrics and benchmarks

scenes.title: Evaluating generative AI
scenes.sub: Automatic metrics, model judges, people and benchmarks
scenes.say: A classifier is right or wrong. A generated answer can be correct, partly correct, unsafe, unfaithful to its sources, or simply unhelpful. | This video covers how generative AI is evaluated, what benchmarks can and can’t tell you, and how security evaluation differs.

scenes.title: Why generative output is hard to score

items.d: Two very different summaries can both be correct
Correct, grounded, safe, helpful, well formatted
The same test can pass on one run and fail on the next
A small prompt change can shift results

scenes.say: Generative output is hard to score for four reasons. | There are many right answers. Two summaries can use completely different words and both be excellent. | Quality has many dimensions: correctness, faithfulness to sources, safety, helpfulness and format. | Output varies from run to run, so one test run proves little. | And results are sensitive to wording: rephrase the prompt slightly, and scores can move.

scenes.title: Three ways to evaluate
rows: Compare output to a reference, or run tests
A strong model scores output against a rubric
Experts rate or compare outputs
Cheap, fast, repeatable
Scales, and captures meaning
The best judge of real quality
Misses meaning; rewards word overlap
Biased, and can itself be manipulated
Slow, costly and inconsistent
scenes.say: There are three broad ways to evaluate generative output. | Automatic metrics compare output with a reference answer, or run objective tests. A model as judge uses a strong language model to score outputs against a rubric. Human review uses experts to rate or compare outputs. | Automatic metrics are cheap and repeatable. Model judges scale well and capture meaning. Human review remains the best judge of real-world quality. | But automatic metrics miss meaning and reward word overlap. Model judges have biases, such as favouring longer answers, and can be manipulated by text in the output they grade. And human review is slow, costly and inconsistent between reviewers. Mature teams combine all three.

scenes.title: Common automatic metrics

items.d: Short factual answers compared with a reference
Word overlap for translation and summarisation
Chance that at least one of k code samples passes the tests
How well a model predicts text: lower is better

scenes.say: You will meet a handful of automatic metrics. | Exact match and token-level F1 compare short factual answers with a reference. | BLEU and ROUGE measure word overlap with reference text, BLEU traditionally for translation and ROUGE for summarisation. | pass at k, used for code, is the probability that at least one of k generated samples passes the unit tests. | And perplexity measures how well a model predicts a sample of text. Lower is better, but it says nothing about whether answers are true or safe.

scenes.title: Evaluating a RAG system

items.d: Did it fetch the passages that contain the answer?
Is every claim supported by the retrieved passages?
Does it actually answer the question asked?
Does it decline when the sources don’t say?

scenes.say: RAG systems need their own measures, because failures can happen at each stage. | Retrieval quality asks whether the system fetched the passages that actually contain the answer. | Faithfulness, sometimes called groundedness, asks whether every claim in the answer is supported by those passages. | Answer relevance asks whether the response actually addresses the question. | And correct abstention asks whether the system says it doesn’t know when the sources don’t contain the answer. Measuring these separately tells you whether to fix retrieval or generation.

scenes.title: Why benchmark scores mislead

items.d: Test questions leaked into the training data
Top models all score near the ceiling
A measure that becomes a target stops measuring
Your data, users and risks aren’t in the benchmark

scenes.say: Public benchmarks, such as MMLU for broad knowledge, HumanEval for code and TruthfulQA for resisting popular misconceptions, let you compare models. But treat the scores with care. | Contamination happens when benchmark questions end up in the training data, so the model has effectively seen the exam paper. | Saturation means the best models all score near the ceiling, so the benchmark no longer separates them. | Goodhart’s law applies: when a measure becomes a target, developers optimise for the benchmark rather than the capability. | And no public benchmark contains your data, your users or your risks. Always evaluate on your own representative test set.

scenes.title: Evaluating security and safety

items.d: Share of adversarial attempts that succeed
Refuses what it should, without over-refusing
System prompt, personal data, other tenants’ data
Paraphrases, typos, other languages, long inputs
Report rates over many runs, not a single pass

scenes.say: Security and safety evaluation asks different questions. | Attack success rate is the share of adversarial attempts, such as injection or jailbreak attempts from a test library, that succeed. | Refusal balance checks that the system refuses harmful requests, without over-refusing legitimate ones, which pushes users towards unsanctioned tools. | Leakage tests check that system prompts, personal data and other tenants’ data stay protected. | Robustness tests repeat the same intent with paraphrases, typos, other languages and very long inputs. | And because output varies, every test is repeated, and results are reported as rates over many runs.

items: Generative quality has many dimensions
Combine automatic metrics, model judges and people
RAG: retrieval, faithfulness, relevance, abstention
Benchmarks compare models; your own tests decide
scenes.say: To recap. | Generative quality has many dimensions, so no single score is enough. | Combine automatic metrics, model judges and human review, each where it is strongest. | Evaluate RAG systems stage by stage: retrieval, faithfulness, relevance and abstention. | And use public benchmarks to shortlist models, but let evaluation on your own data, including adversarial tests, make the decision.

blocks.md:
### Three families of evaluation
**Automatic, reference-based metrics** compare output with one or more reference answers.
- **Exact match** and token-level **F1** suit short factual answers.
- **BLEU** (translation) and **ROUGE** (summarisation) count overlapping words and phrases with a reference. They are cheap and repeatable but reward surface similarity: a fluent paraphrase can score badly, and a wrong answer that reuses the reference’s words can score well.
- **Embedding-based similarity** (for example, BERTScore) compares meaning rather than exact words.
- **pass@k** runs generated code against unit tests and estimates the probability that at least one of *k* samples passes. Objective tests like these are the most trustworthy automatic measures where they exist.
- **Perplexity** measures how well a model predicts held-out text. It is useful when training models but says nothing about truth, safety or helpfulness.

**Model-graded evaluation (LLM as a judge)** asks a strong model to score outputs against a rubric, or to choose the better of two outputs. It scales to thousands of cases and captures meaning, but it has known biases:
- **position bias** (favouring the first or second option),
- **verbosity bias** (favouring longer answers),
- **self-preference** (favouring outputs from its own model family),
- and susceptibility to **manipulation**: text inside the output being graded can try to instruct the judge.

Mitigations include clear rubrics, swapping the order of options, using a different model family as the judge, isolating graded content from judge instructions, and **calibrating the judge against a sample of human ratings**.

**Human evaluation** uses experts or representative users to rate outputs or compare pairs. It remains the reference standard for quality, but it is slow and costly, and raters disagree. Good practice is to write clear guidelines, use several raters and measure their agreement.

### Benchmarks
| Benchmark | What it tests |
|---|---|
| **MMLU** | Multiple-choice knowledge across 57 subjects, from law to physics |
| **HumanEval** | Writing Python functions that pass unit tests (scored with pass@k) |
| **TruthfulQA** | Avoiding false answers that mimic popular misconceptions |
| **GSM8K** | Multi-step grade-school maths word problems |
| **HELM** | A holistic framework reporting many metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, toxicity, efficiency) across many scenarios |
| **Crowdsourced arenas** | People compare two anonymous models’ answers; ratings are computed from many pairwise votes |

Benchmarks are useful for shortlisting models and tracking progress, but they mislead in predictable ways:
- **Contamination:** benchmark items are published online and can leak into training data, inflating scores.
- **Saturation:** when leading models all score near the maximum, the benchmark stops discriminating, and harder successors replace it.
- **Goodhart’s law:** optimising for a benchmark can improve the score without improving the underlying capability.
- **Relevance:** your users, data, languages and threats are not in the benchmark.

### Evaluating in your own context
A sound evaluation programme for a generative AI application usually includes:
1. **A golden dataset:** representative questions with approved answers or rubrics, drawn from real use.
2. **Edge cases:** unanswerable questions, outdated information, ambiguous requests and multiple languages.
3. **Adversarial cases:** prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, data-extraction attempts and harmful requests, drawn from maintained test libraries.
4. **Over-refusal cases:** legitimate requests that look superficially risky, to check the system doesn’t refuse them.
5. **Repeated runs:** each case run several times, with results reported as rates.
6. **Regression discipline:** the suite re-runs on every change of model, prompt, retrieval configuration or guardrail, and on a schedule.

This is the **Measure** function of the NIST AI RMF in practice: defining metrics, testing before deployment, and continuing to measure in production.

blocks.title: Match the metric to its use
pairs: pass@k
Generated code checked by unit tests
ROUGE
Overlap between a summary and a reference summary
Faithfulness (groundedness)
Whether a RAG answer’s claims are supported by retrieved passages
Attack success rate
Share of adversarial attempts that achieve their goal
Perplexity
How well a model predicts held-out text

blocks.title: Pitfalls when a model grades another model
items: Position and verbosity bias
Judges tend to favour whichever answer appears in a particular position, and longer answers. Swap the order and average the results, and penalise padding in the rubric.
Self-preference
Judges may favour outputs from their own model family. Use a judge from a different family for comparisons between vendors.
Manipulation through the graded output
An output can contain text aimed at the judge, such as a claim that it deserves full marks. Keep graded content clearly separated from the judge’s instructions, and spot-check high scores.
Drift in the judge
If the judge model is updated, scores change even though the system under test did not. Pin the judge’s version and re-calibrate against human ratings when it changes.

q.q: A vendor says its model is “state of the art” because it tops a well-known public benchmark. What is the BEST next step before choosing it for your customer-service assistant?
o: Accept the claim, because public benchmarks are run independently and so can’t be inflated by the vendor
Test it on your own representative and adversarial cases, since public scores can be inflated by contamination
Choose whichever model has the highest perplexity on the benchmark, since that measures its confidence
Ask the vendor for a second, independent public benchmark score, and choose the model if the two results agree
q.why: Public benchmarks help shortlist models, but contamination, saturation and Goodhart effects can inflate scores, and none reflect your data, users or threats. Your own evaluation decides.

sections.title: Operational modes: human in the loop or automated?

scenes.title: Who decides: person or machine?
scenes.sub: Human in the loop, on the loop, and fully automated
scenes.say: Given everything we know about AI’s limits, how much should we let it decide on its own? | This video covers the operational modes for AI decisions, how to choose between them, and how to keep human oversight from becoming a rubber stamp.

scenes.title: Three operational modes

items.d: The AI recommends; a person approves each decision before it takes effect
The AI acts; people monitor and can intervene or override
No person reviews individual decisions; people set policy and audit

scenes.say: There are three main operational modes. | With a human in the loop, the AI recommends and a person approves each decision before it takes effect. A credit analyst signing off a loan decision is the classic example. | With a human on the loop, the AI acts on its own while people monitor it and can step in, override or stop it, like a security team watching an automated blocking system. | With automated execution, no person reviews individual decisions. People still set policies, thresholds and limits, and audit results in aggregate, as with spam filtering.

scenes.title: Choosing the mode
rows: High impact
Low impact
scenes.say: How do you choose? Two questions do most of the work: how much impact does the decision have on people, and how easily can it be reversed? | High impact and hard to reverse, such as denying a benefit, firing an employee or deleting production data, calls for a human in the loop. | High impact but easy to reverse, such as temporarily holding a suspicious payment, can run with a human on the loop. | Low impact but hard to reverse still deserves monitoring, with a human on the loop. | And low impact, easily reversed decisions, such as routing a support ticket, can be automated and audited. Confidence, volume, regulation and the maturity of the model then fine-tune the choice.

scenes.title: Routing by confidence and impact

note.text: Confidence routing only works if the model is calibrated.

scenes.say: Many systems mix the modes. A case arrives and the model produces a decision with a confidence score. | Routing rules combine confidence with the impact of the decision. | Confident, low-impact cases are actioned automatically, with a random sample audited by people. | Uncertain or high-impact cases go to a person, who sees the evidence behind the recommendation and has real authority to override it. | Remember Section 1: this only works if the model’s confidence is calibrated. An overconfident model routes its worst mistakes straight past the humans.

scenes.title: When oversight becomes a rubber stamp

items.d: People defer to the machine, even when it is wrong
Hundreds of reviews an hour leaves seconds each
The reviewer sees the verdict but not the reasons
Overriding is discouraged, slow or penalised

scenes.say: A human in the loop only helps if the human genuinely decides. Oversight degrades into a rubber stamp in four common ways. | Automation bias: people tend to defer to automated recommendations, even when they have evidence the machine is wrong. | No time to think: a reviewer handling hundreds of cases an hour has seconds for each. | No evidence: the reviewer sees the verdict but not the information behind it, so there is nothing to disagree with. | And no real authority: overriding the system is discouraged, slow, or counts against the reviewer.

scenes.title: Making oversight meaningful

items.d: Reasons, sources and confidence alongside the recommendation
Competence, time, and the authority to say no
Near-zero suggests rubber-stamping; very high suggests a poor model
Anyone overseeing can halt the system safely

scenes.say: Here is how to make oversight real. | Show the evidence: the reasons, sources and confidence behind each recommendation, not just a verdict. | Train reviewers, give them enough time, and make sure they have the authority to say no. | Measure override rates. A rate near zero suggests rubber-stamping; a very high rate suggests the model isn’t fit for purpose. Both deserve investigation. | And keep a stop button: overseers must be able to halt the system safely. The EU AI Act requires exactly these capabilities for high-risk systems, including awareness of automation bias and the ability to interrupt the system.

items: HITL approves each decision; HOTL monitors and intervenes
Choose by impact and reversibility, then confidence
Beware automation bias and rubber-stamping
Evidence, authority, override metrics and a stop button
scenes.say: To recap. | With a human in the loop, a person approves each decision; on the loop, people monitor and intervene; automated execution relies on policy and audit. | Choose the mode by impact and reversibility first, then by confidence, volume and regulation. | Beware automation bias and rubber-stamping. | And make oversight meaningful with evidence, trained and empowered reviewers, override metrics and a stop button.

blocks.md:
### The modes in more detail
| Mode | Who decides each case | Typical uses | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Human in the loop (HITL)** | A person, after reviewing the AI’s recommendation | Credit and benefit decisions, medical diagnosis support, high-value payments, agent actions with external effect | Rubber-stamping; slow throughput |
| **Human on the loop (HOTL)** | The AI, under real-time human supervision with power to intervene | Automated threat blocking, fraud holds, content moderation queues, agents acting within limits | Monitoring fatigue; intervention too late |
| **Automated execution** (human out of the loop) | The AI, within policies and limits set by people | Spam filtering, ticket routing, low-value recommendations | Unnoticed systematic errors |

Some frameworks also describe **human in command**: people retain overall control over whether, when and how a system is used, including the decision to switch it off. This applies whatever the per-decision mode.

### Choosing the mode
Start with two questions:
1. **Impact:** how badly can a wrong decision affect people, money, safety or rights?
2. **Reversibility:** can a wrong decision be undone quickly and completely?

Then refine with:
- **Confidence and calibration:** can the model reliably tell when it might be wrong?
- **Volume and speed:** can people realistically review every case, and does the decision need to happen faster than a person can act (for example, blocking malware in milliseconds)?
- **Regulation:** some decisions legally require human involvement.
- **Maturity:** a new model usually starts with more oversight and earns autonomy as evidence of performance builds up.

### A progression towards autonomy
Organisations rarely jump straight to automation. A common progression is:
1. **Shadow mode:** the model runs on live cases but takes no action; its decisions are compared with human decisions.
2. **Assist mode:** the model recommends; people decide every case (HITL).
3. **Supervised automation:** the model acts on confident, low-impact cases; people handle the rest and monitor (HOTL).
4. **Automated execution:** the model acts within limits; people audit samples and aggregate metrics.

Each step should be a governed decision with agreed criteria, such as accuracy on recent cases, override rates and incident history, and each step should be reversible if monitoring shows problems.

### What the law says
- **GDPR Article 22** gives people the right not to be subject to a decision based *solely* on automated processing that produces legal or similarly significant effects, subject to exceptions. Where such decisions are allowed, safeguards include the right to obtain human intervention, to express a point of view and to contest the decision. A token human who rubber-stamps every output does not make a decision any less “solely automated”.
- **EU AI Act Article 14** requires high-risk AI systems to be designed for effective human oversight, proportionate to the risks and the system’s level of autonomy. The people overseeing a system must be able to understand its capabilities and limitations, monitor its operation, **remain aware of automation bias**, correctly interpret its output, decide not to use it or to override or reverse its output, and **interrupt it through a stop button or similar procedure**. For certain remote biometric identification systems, a match must be separately verified by at least two people before action is taken.

### Agents raise the stakes
Agents (Module 1.2) take actions rather than give answers, often many per minute. Apply the same logic per *action*: reading a calendar can be automated; sending an external email might run on the loop; making a payment, deleting data or changing access rights should require approval. Domain 4 covers how to enforce this in the orchestration layer.

blocks.title: Which mode would you choose?
items: Blocking known malware
**Automated execution, audited.** Decisions are needed in milliseconds, volumes are huge, and a wrongly quarantined file can be restored. Monitor false-positive reports and sample decisions.
Holding a suspicious payment
**Human on the loop.** Holding the payment for a few hours is reversible and limits loss. Analysts review holds promptly and release or confirm them.
Denying a mortgage application
**Human in the loop.** The decision has significant effects on a person and is subject to legal safeguards. The model informs; a trained underwriter decides, with the evidence in front of them.
Agent deleting cloud resources
**Human in the loop for each deletion.** Deletion is hard to reverse and can cause outages. The agent can propose a clean-up plan; a person approves the specific actions.
Routing support tickets
**Automated execution.** Low impact, easy to correct, high volume. Track misroutes and retrain when they rise.

blocks.title: Spotting the right answer
blocks.md: When a scenario involves **significant effects on people** and **hard-to-reverse** outcomes, the best answer usually adds meaningful human review, not just *any* human. Look for options that give reviewers **evidence, time and authority**. Options that keep a human but add volume targets, hide the model’s reasoning or penalise overrides are traps.

blocks.title: The 99.8% approval rate
blocks.md: An insurer uses a model to recommend whether claims should be paid. A claims handler must approve every recommendation before it takes effect. An audit finds that handlers accept 99.8% of recommendations, spending an average of eight seconds on each, and that handlers who overturned recommendations were flagged for “slow processing”.

q.q: What is the MOST significant problem, and the BEST fix?
o: The model is too accurate, so handlers disengage; deliberately reduce its accuracy so that humans stay alert
Oversight has become a rubber stamp; give handlers evidence, time and freedom to override, and monitor overrides
Remove the human step entirely, since handlers add no value and only slow down decisions that the model gets right
Add a second handler to approve every case in eight seconds, so that two people sign off every decision
q.why: The pattern shows automation bias reinforced by incentives against overriding. The fix is to make oversight meaningful: evidence, time, authority and monitoring. Removing the human may also breach legal requirements for decisions with significant effects, and a second rushed reviewer adds cost without adding judgement.

q.q: An AI system acts on its own, while a team monitors its decisions in real time and can intervene, override or stop it. Which operational mode is this?
o: Human in the loop
Human on the loop
Shadow mode
Human out of the loop with no monitoring
q.why: Human on the loop means the system acts autonomously under supervision, with people able to intervene. Human in the loop would require approval before each decision takes effect.

quiz.q: A research assistant confidently cites a court decision that does not exist. What is this failure called?
o: Prompt injection (indirect)
Hallucination (confabulation)
Concept drift (model decay)
Training data poisoning
quiz.why: Fluent, plausible but fabricated output is hallucination, which the NIST Generative AI Profile calls confabulation. No attacker or data change is needed for it to happen.

quiz.q: A summary states that a project was approved, but the source report says it was rejected. Which type of hallucination is this?
o: Extrinsic hallucination
Intrinsic hallucination
Aleatoric uncertainty
Model collapse
quiz.why: An intrinsic hallucination contradicts the source the model was given. An extrinsic hallucination adds claims the source cannot support.

quiz.q: Why can an LLM produce slightly different outputs for the same prompt even with temperature set to 0?
o: Temperature 0 maximises randomness, so the model deliberately picks a different token each time
Floating-point operations can run in different orders across hardware and batches, and providers may update models
The model permanently learns from every request, so each new answer reflects the previous conversations
Tokens are randomly reassigned to new IDs on each call, so the same prompt is encoded differently every time
quiz.why: Low temperature removes most sampling randomness, but numerical differences from batching and hardware, and provider-side changes, can still alter outputs.

quiz.q: Which type of uncertainty can be reduced by collecting more or better training data?
o: Aleatoric uncertainty
Epistemic uncertainty
Irreducible measurement noise
Label ambiguity in the data itself
quiz.why: Epistemic uncertainty reflects gaps in the model’s knowledge and shrinks with better data. Aleatoric uncertainty is inherent noise or ambiguity in the data.

quiz.q: A hosted LLM application starts answering differently after the provider updates the model behind the same API name. What is this called?
o: Concept drift
Behavioural drift
Model collapse
Label (prior) shift
quiz.why: Behavioural drift is a change in a generative system’s outputs caused by changes to the model, prompts, retrieval or tools. Version pinning and regression testing control it.

quiz.q: Which monitoring approach gives the EARLIEST warning that a model is seeing inputs unlike its training data?
o: Waiting for the quarterly accuracy report, which shows whether predictions are still correct
Comparing production input distributions with the training baseline using statistics such as PSI
Counting how many model versions have been deployed since the original training run
Reviewing the training code each month to confirm that nothing in the pipeline has changed since launch
quiz.why: Input distribution monitoring needs no labels, so it detects data drift immediately. Performance metrics need true outcomes, which often arrive late.

o: A sudden outage of a model-serving cluster when demand exceeds the available accelerator capacity
Progressive degradation when models train on earlier models’ outputs, losing rare patterns and diversity
The loss of earlier skills when a model is fine-tuned on a new task, also called catastrophic forgetting
A model refusing too many harmless requests after safety tuning has been applied too aggressively
quiz.why: Model collapse results from recursive training on model-generated data. Losing earlier skills during new training is catastrophic forgetting, a different problem.

quiz.q: Which control MOST directly reduces the risk of model collapse?
o: Training each new model only on the previous model’s outputs, which are cleaner than human data
Tracking data provenance and keeping and accumulating genuine human data alongside any synthetic data
Raising the model’s temperature during data generation so that synthetic outputs are more varied and diverse
Deleting older human training data to save storage and keep each training set focused on recent outputs
quiz.why: Provenance lets you know what is synthetic, and accumulating rather than replacing real data preserves the tails of the distribution.

quiz.q: For a malware detector, which metric measures the share of actual malware that was detected?
o: Precision
Recall rate
Specificity
Accuracy
quiz.why: Recall (sensitivity, true positive rate) is TP ÷ (TP + FN): the proportion of real positives caught. Precision is the proportion of alerts that are real.

quiz.q: A detector produces 200 alerts, of which 50 are real attacks. What is its precision?
quiz.why: Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP) = 50 ÷ 200 = 25%. Three in four alerts are false positives.

o: Malware hidden in benchmark software that tampers with the scores it reports
Benchmark test items appearing in a model’s training data, inflating its score
Benchmarks that mix too many languages, which makes the results hard to compare
A benchmark run on unpatched hardware, which leaves the evaluation results open to tampering
quiz.why: If a model has seen the test items during training, its score reflects memorisation rather than capability.

quiz.q: Reviewers approve 99.8% of AI recommendations, spending a few seconds on each. Which risk does this MOST suggest?
o: Model collapse from synthetic data
Automation bias and rubber-stamp oversight
Data drift in the recommendations
Unbounded token consumption during the review
quiz.why: Near-universal, very fast approval suggests reviewers are deferring to the system rather than exercising judgement, which defeats the purpose of a human in the loop.

exam.q: Two analysts use the same LLM tool to summarise the same incident ticket and receive noticeably different summaries. What is the BEST first step?
o: Report the tool to the vendor as compromised, since a sound model should give identical summaries
Check the logged model version, prompt and sampling settings, then standardise them for this task
Ban the tool for incident work immediately until the vendor can guarantee fully deterministic outputs
Retrain the model on the organisation’s own incident tickets so it learns a single house summary style
exam.why: Variation is expected from sampling, version changes and context differences. Diagnosing the cause from logs and then pinning versions, lowering temperature and standardising prompts is proportionate. Treating it as a compromise or retraining is premature.

exam.q: A developer installs a library recommended by a code assistant. The library name was invented by the model, and an attacker had registered it with malicious code. How is this BEST classified?
o: A pure model limitation with no security relevance, because the model itself never installed anything
A hallucination that became a supply-chain vulnerability because the output was used without verification
A denial-of-service attack on the code assistant, because its recommendations were deliberately flooded
Concept drift in the code assistant, because package ecosystems changed after its training cut-off date
exam.why: Hallucinated package names are a limitation; attackers exploit them by registering the names. Dependency verification turns the limitation back into a harmless error.

exam.q: A fraud model’s precision has declined steadily for three months, but its input distributions are stable. True fraud labels arrive about 60 days after each transaction. What is the MOST likely cause and BEST response?
o: Data drift; collect more recent inputs and retrain immediately on the unlabelled transactions as they arrive
Concept drift; retrain on recent labelled data, and watch leading indicators such as overrides while labels lag
Model collapse; find and delete any synthetic transactions that have entered the training data pipeline
Label drift; lower the decision threshold sharply so the model flags far more transactions as fraud
exam.why: Stable inputs with falling performance points to a changed relationship between inputs and outcomes: concept drift. Because labels are delayed, leading indicators help detect it sooner.

exam.q: Which event should MOST clearly trigger re-evaluation of a deployed LLM application before it continues in production?
o: A scheduled backup of the application’s vector index, prompts and configuration completing successfully
The provider announcing that a new model version will replace the current one behind the same endpoint
A redesign of the colour scheme and layout of the user interface that the assistant is embedded in
A 20% increase in the number of employees who are licensed to use the application each month
exam.why: A model change can alter behaviour, including safety behaviour. The golden test set and safety evaluations should be re-run before accepting it.

exam.q: A company plans to train its next customer-support model mainly on conversations generated by its current model and to discard older human transcripts. Average answer-quality scores are expected to stay the same. What is the BEST advice?
o: Proceed, because average answer quality is the measure that matters most to customers and the business
Keep and accumulate human transcripts, label and limit synthetic data, verify it, and test rare and hard cases
Use a different vendor’s model to generate the synthetic conversations, so the training data is more diverse
Generate ten times more synthetic conversations, so the extra volume compensates for losing the human data
exam.why: Replacing real data with recursive synthetic data risks model collapse, which hides behind stable averages. Provenance, accumulation, curation and tail evaluation are the mitigations.

exam.q: A SOC is tuning an AI alert-triage model. Analysts can handle about 200 escalations a day, and a missed intrusion is very costly. How should the decision threshold be set?
o: Maximise overall accuracy, since that balances missed intrusions against false alarms
Maximise precision regardless of recall, so that analysts only ever see alerts that are genuine incidents
Favour recall within analyst capacity, and measure both precision and recall at the chosen threshold
Leave the default threshold of 0.5, because the vendor has already calibrated it for SOCs
exam.why: Costly misses call for high recall, constrained by realistic alert volume. Accuracy is misleading for rare events, and a default threshold ignores the cost of errors.

exam.q: A team evaluates a RAG assistant using an LLM judge. Scores are excellent, but users complain of unsupported answers. Investigation shows answers contain text praising their own accuracy. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Ask the judge to be much stricter by adding firm instructions to penalise any answer that praises its own accuracy
Isolate graded text from judge instructions, check faithfulness to sources, and calibrate against human ratings
Replace the LLM judge with BLEU scores, which compare each answer’s wording with a reference answer
Stop automated evaluation and rely on user complaints, which reflect real problems more accurately
exam.why: Model judges can be biased and manipulated by the content they grade. Isolation, task-specific faithfulness checks and human calibration make the evaluation trustworthy.

exam.q: An insurer automatically denies some claims based on a model’s output, with significant effects on claimants. What is MOST important from a compliance and governance perspective?
o: Publishing the model’s overall accuracy on the company website so claimants can judge its reliability
Ensuring meaningful human review is available, by reviewers with the evidence, time and authority to change it
Raising the model’s confidence threshold to 99%, so that only very certain denials are issued automatically
Adding a clear disclaimer to denial letters explaining that the decision was produced by an AI model
exam.why: Decisions with legal or similarly significant effects attract safeguards such as the right to human intervention (for example, GDPR Article 22). Oversight must be meaningful, not a rubber stamp.
